extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in mathematics studying PDE and thermodynamics (course/lecture notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style mathematical treatment of entropy: axiomatic thermodynamics (equilibrium and processes), thermodynamic potentials, Carnot cycles, Clausius inequality, and connections between entropy concepts and elliptic/parabolic PDE, conservation laws, Hamilton–Jacobi equations, and large deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model for a thermal system in equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose given (a) an open, convex subset Σ of R^{m+1}, and (b) a C^1-function S : Σ → R such that (i) S is concave, (ii) ∂S/∂E > 0, (iii) S is positively homogeneous of degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the axiomatic starting model used throughout Chapters I–III. Homogeneity encodes extensivity (additivity over subsystems); positivity of ∂S/∂E encodes positive temperature; concavity follows from the Second Law/entropy additivity when combining isolated bodies. All subsequent derived quantities are defined on regions where these hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental equation
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula S = S(E, X1, …, Xm) is called the fundamental equation of our system and by definition contains all the thermodynamic information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish fundamental equation (complete thermodynamic information) from equations of state (identities involving derived quantities that typically do not contain all information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of internal energy E
rubrics_metrics.description: Because ∂S/∂E > 0 one can solve for E as a C^1 function of (S, X1, …, Xm): E = E(S, X1, …, Xm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E is called the internal energy; existence/regularity follows from monotonicity of S in E. Many formulas and definitions (T, Pk) are given in terms of derivatives of E.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of temperature and generalized forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Define T = ∂E/∂S (temperature) and P_k = -∂E/∂X_k (kth generalized force / pressure). Also ∂S/∂E = 1/T and ∂S/∂X_k = P_k/T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These relations (and Lemmas 1–2) provide the bridge between derivatives of E and S and physically interpretable intensive variables; use them to derive Gibbs' formula and other identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gibbs' formula
rubrics_metrics.description: dE = T dS - Σ_{k=1}^m P_k dX_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this point Gibbs' formula is purely a differential identity (no dynamics assumed). In later chapters T dS and Σ P_k dX_k are interpreted as 'infinitesimal heating' and 'infinitesimal working' respectively when processes are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive and intensive parameters (homogeneity implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: S and E are extensive (positively homogeneous of degree 1); X1,…,Xm are extensive; T and P_k are intensive (positively homogeneous of degree 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneity implies additivity over subregions and that intensive variables take the same value on subregions in equilibrium. Use scaling properties to check consistency of thermodynamic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concavity of entropy
rubrics_metrics.description: S is a concave function of (E, X1, …, Xm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivated by the Second Law: combining two isolated bodies and allowing them to equilibrate cannot decrease total entropy, which implies concavity. This property underlies many variational statements and stability results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity of energy
rubrics_metrics.description: E is a convex function of (S, X1, …, Xm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convexity of E follows from concavity of S and the invertibility relationship between E and S. Convexity/concavity are central to Legendre transform constructions and stability/uniqueness of dual potentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy maximization and energy minimization principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Entropy Maximization Principle: The equilibrium value of any unconstrained internal parameter is such as to maximize the entropy for the given value of total internal energy. Energy Minimization Principle: The equilibrium value of any unconstrained internal parameter is such as to minimize the energy for the given value of total entropy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dual variational principles give operational methods to locate equilibrium states under constraints; graphical illustrations link them to Legendre duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermodynamic potentials via Legendre transform
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Helmholtz free energy F(T,V) = inf_S (E(S,V) - T S), enthalpy H(S,P) = inf_V (E(S,V) + P V), and Gibbs potential G(T,P) = inf_{S,V} (E(S,V) + P V - S T). Equivalently when infima are attained: F = E - T S, H = E + P V, G = E - T S + P V with appropriate solves for conjugate variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use convex analysis (Legendre transform) with the sign conventions customary in thermodynamics (negative of mathematical transform in places). Assumptions of strict convexity and unique attainment (E C^2, strictly convex and inf attained uniquely) allow rewriting inf forms as explicit functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convexity/concavity properties of thermodynamic potentials and Maxwell relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under E C^2 strictly convex and unique inf attainment: (i) E locally strictly convex in (S,V); (ii) F locally strictly concave in T and strictly convex in V; (iii) H locally strictly concave in P and strictly convex in S; (iv) G locally strictly concave in (T,P). Mixed partial equalities yield Maxwell relations (identities equating mixed second derivatives of E, F, G, H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maxwell relations (e.g., ∂^2E/∂V∂S = ∂^2E/∂S∂V, and the corresponding relations for F,G,H) are consequences of equality of mixed derivatives and are useful for deriving thermodynamic identities and interrelations among measurable quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of capacities and thermodynamic coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Define heat capacities: C_P = T (∂S/∂T)_P, C_V = T (∂S/∂T)_V; latent heats Λ_P,T and Λ_V,T via T ∂S/∂P and T ∂S/∂V; coefficient of thermal expansion β = (1/V)(∂V/∂T)_P; compressibilities K_T = - (1/V)(∂V/∂P)_T and K_S = - (1/V)(∂V/∂P)_S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relations among these quantities include C_P ≥ C_V > 0, C_P - C_V = T * ( (∂P/∂T)_V )^2 / ( -∂P/∂V |_T ) (Kelvin/Maxwell-type identities). These identities are derived from properties of F,G and Maxwell relations and are useful checks on models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal gas equation of state and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal gas (N=1): P V = R T. Consequences: C_P, C_V depend only on T; C_P - C_V = R; E = E(T) = ∫_{T0}^T C_V(θ) dθ + E0; S(T,V) = R log V + ∫_{T0}^T C_V(θ)/θ dθ + S0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a simple ideal gas (C_V constant), explicit closed-form expressions follow: E = C_V T, S = R log V + C_V log T + constant. Check concavity of S in (E,V) via second derivatives in simple models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Van der Waals fluid model and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Van der Waals equation for N=1: P = R T/(V - b) - a/V^2. Consequences: C_V depends only on T; E(T,V) = ∫ C_V + (-a/V) + const; S(T,V) = R log(V - b) + ∫ C_V/θ dθ + const. However S(E,V) may not be concave everywhere (phase transitions) so restrict to regions Σ where concavity holds or take concave envelope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use van der Waals as an example showing failure of global concavity and the thermodynamic interpretation of phase transitions; use concave envelope for physical interpretations when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model for a homogeneous fluid body (dynamic/process viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: State space Σ ⊂ (0,∞)×(0,∞) with C^1 functions P(T,V), Λ_V(T,V), C_V(T,V) given and assumptions ∂P/∂V < 0, Λ_V ≠ 0, C_V > 0 on Σ. Paths Γ are oriented continuous piecewise C^1 curves in Σ; cycles are closed paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the starting point for process-level thermodynamics (Chapter II). Explicit regularity and sign conditions are required to construct energy and entropy from process integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working and heating 1-forms; path-dependent work/heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Define working 1-form d^-W = P dV and heating 1-form d^-Q = C_V dT + Λ_V dV. The work W(Γ) = ∫_Γ P dV and heat Q(Γ) = ∫_Γ (C_V dT + Λ_V dV) depend on the path Γ (not only endpoints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The slashed differential notation emphasizes non-exactness in general. Distinguish isothermal paths (T constant) and adiabatic paths (q(t)=0 where q is pointwise heating rate). Adiabatic paths satisfy ODE dV/dT = -C_V / Λ_V when parameterized as V(T).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Law for cycles and existence of internal energy E
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume for every cycle Γ that W(Γ) = Q(Γ). Then the 1-form C_V dT + (Λ_V - P) dV is exact on Σ (open, simply connected), hence there exists C^2 function E(T,V) with ∂E/∂T = C_V and ∂E/∂V = Λ_V - P; equivalently dE = d^-Q - d^-W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the process-level statement of energy conservation that yields internal energy as a state function when cycle integrals of net heat and work balance for all cycles. Units consistency (mechanical equivalent of heat) may be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnot cycle and Carnot heat engine definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A Carnot cycle Γ consists of two adiabatic and two isothermal paths. It is a Carnot heat engine when heat Q+ is gained at higher temperature T2 and heat Q- is lost at lower temperature T1, with net work W = Q+ - Q- > 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ideal gas Carnot engine calculations give Q+ = R T2 log(V2/V1), Q- = R T1 log(V4/V3) and W = (1 - T1/T2) Q+. The efficiency relation W/Q+ = 1 - T1/T2 is derived in the model example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law (Carnot/Clausius form) and existence of entropy S
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a Second Law hypothesis concerning Carnot engines (Clausius-type statement) which leads to the existence of an entropy function S and inequalities expressing irreversibility (Clausius inequality); entropy is nondecreasing for irreversible processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the detailed Second Law text is in later parts of the chapter, the notes indicate that under appropriate Carnot/Clausius hypotheses one can define S so that dS = dQ/T for reversible processes and that Q/T integrals satisfy the Clausius inequality for general processes. This provides a construction/characterization of entropy from process-level axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legendre transform and convex duality prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: For convex analysis: let H : R^n → (-∞,+∞] be proper, convex, lower semicontinuous; define Legendre transform L(q) = sup_{p∈R^n} (p·q - H(p)). Then L is convex, l.s.c., and H = L^*; for C^2 strictly convex H, the maximizing p satisfies q = D H(p) and D L(q) = p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard convex-analytic machinery is used repeatedly to define thermodynamic potentials and understand duality between entropy/energy representations; check regularity and strict convexity assumptions when applying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of entropy concepts in PDE (elliptic/parabolic/conservation laws/Hamilton–Jacobi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Entropy concepts are used to: interpret PDE estimates (e.g., Clausius inequality analogues for linear second-order elliptic and parabolic PDE), define entropy/entropy-flux pairs and entropy solutions for conservation laws, link viscosity solutions/Hopf–Lax formula to entropy and to diffusion limits, and relate entropy to probabilistic notions (H-theorem, large deviations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout Chapters IV–VI and V the notes outline how inequalities inherent in weak-solution definitions correspond to irreversibility/entropy conditions; this provides a unifying criterion when analyzing PDE models — verify appropriate entropy inequalities, entropy production estimates, and compatibility with variational principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callen's physical postulates (axioms for equilibrium thermodynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulate I: Equilibrium states are characterized completely by internal energy E and extensive parameters X1,…,Xm. Postulate II: There exists an entropy function of the extensive parameters; unconstrained values maximize entropy subject to constraints. Postulate III: Entropy is additive over subsystems, homogeneous of first order, continuous, differentiable and monotone increasing in energy. Postulate IV (Third Law): Entropy vanishes in the state with T = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These postulates (quoted from Callen) form the foundational criteria for equilibrium thermodynamics used in the notes; Postulate IV (Third Law) is noted but not included in the models here. Use these as axiomatic checks when building thermodynamic models.
